english_verification.review_scope: Representative current-Mod opening identity, formation and Deioderan sources; exact source names and selected English Wiki passages; no exhaustive mission audit or national-idea retranslation. Native English national-idea names and descriptions were compared by localisation key by the primary. Large source intervals are locator envelopes, not a claim to inspect every intervening line or establish complete runtime reachability.
unresolved: The Jadd page is explicitly still being worked on and does not establish a complete religious history.
Wiki setting dates and post-Deioderan decline are not inevitable player outcomes.
Great Holy War CB, some event tails and exact special-unit unlock dates were not exhaustively checked.

rationale.campaign_length: 21 mission groups and 120 missions span several major regions.
rationale.colonization: Overseas colonisation is not the traditional core loop.
rationale.complexity: Zeal, formation, conversion, court orientation and optional Deioderan are tightly connected.
rationale.dark_story: Religious conquest and civil war include ethnic suspicion and the risk of violence.
rationale.difficulty: Expansion, capacity, conversion and crisis preparation must be managed simultaneously.
rationale.diplomacy: Subjects, ethnic inclusion and diplomatic reunification during Deioderan provide a moderate diplomatic layer.
rationale.early_pressure: The army is strong, but the country needs active wars and loses zeal during peace.
rationale.magic_artifice_intensity: Magic is not the everyday gameplay loop, but the final missions still require a powerful mage and a third-tier Enchantment school.
rationale.narrative_density: Religious expedition, multi-ethnic empire and identity crisis run through the pre- and post-formation campaign.
rationale.tall_play: Temples and capital development matter, but formation and the main route require broad expansion.
rationale.trade_economy: Caravans, imperial trade and the Golden Highway exist, but serve the expansion agenda.
rationale.warfare: High tradition, professionalism, legion zeal and cavalry interaction directly support continuous warfare.

identity.appearance: Starting country in 1444; after satisfying the form_jadd_empire decision, it continues the same campaign chain as the Jadd Empire (F51).

national_ideas.scope_note: National traditions, seven national ideas and ambition only; optional idea groups and racial/government bonuses are excluded. Conditional alternatives are separate, not stacked. Accepting new ideas on formation depends on the actual event/decision and player choice.

description.text: Jaddar realised that the Bulwari Sun Cultists were misguided in their understanding of Surael. The failure of Jaher to do his duty meant that the mission could not rest with a single individual or race, but all races should be incorporated in the duties of Surael. No people should be excluded, so long as they do their part.

description.text: When Jaher's Phoenix Legions returned to Bulwar many of them found a new and strange land that they could not find their home in. They returned to the desert and carved out a new life for themselves in this desolate land. Adapting their battle experience to the wide desert plains, the Phoenix Legions transformed into the mounted Desert Phoenixes.

description.text: Under Jaher's rule, the Phoenix Empire constructed a great road connecting Bulwar to Haless. Over it many goods and troops flowed east and west. This primary artery goes through the heart of our land and we are its guardian. While the road itself may have fallen into disrepair, the route is still there and we control its traffic.

description.text: Jexis, daughter of Jaher, reforged the Phoenix Empire before being assassinated. Unknown to many, she had a son, Jaddar, who is the founder of our nation. While some may disagree about his true heritage, it is clear that we who forged the Phoenix Empire are the true successors of the dynasty.

description.text: Our tolerance of all within the Jadd puts the duties to all within the Jadd. Their duties include that of making others see the light. This responsibility on an individual level takes away some of the burden of spreading the light from the government, allowing for a less hands on approach to the integration of new peoples.

description.text: It is our duty to Surael to banish the dark and spread the light. There are many in the world who do not see this the right way, we shall bring them the truth. If not through word, through fire and blood.

description.text: The followers of the Jadd are full of righteous zeal. We have stimulated their martial zest and now the faithful flock to our banners. The armies of the Jadd will be great and numerous.

description.text: When the Legions adopted the Jadd, they also opened up their ranks to a much greater variety of people and races. While this was initially disruptive and led to a decrease in discipline and organization, it also had as an immediate effect that it greatly increased the manpower pool the state could draw from. This allowed the Jadd Empire to pull on greater amounts of men than their neighbours.

description.text: All within the Jadd are equal and it would not do to suppress any cultures or races. So the Jadd Empire followed a practice of leaving local administrations intact to cause minimal disruption. Where feudal systems existed, the local lords needed to report to the imperial governor, but the rest was left intact. The same occurred with more modern administrations. Only in very tribal systems with no clear power structure was order brought by restructuring the local systems, but local chiefs still stayed in power. Of course all of this was if they did not revolt. This system allowed large areas to be swiftly integrated and reduced the need for forming new local administrations.

description.text: At the heart of the Jadd Empire stood the faith of the Jadd. While proclaiming the empire had given the faith a clear home and base to rally around, the Jadd was not an isolationist religion. Its core tenet was the banishment of the dark, so the Empire ever sought to expand its borders and to spread the faith to new lands. It could not rest until the darkness was banished from all lands.

description.text: The old Phoenix Legions underwent great changes since the Sun Elves first landed on shores of Bulwar. The experience they gained while campaigning through Sarhal and Haless made them strong. The adaptation to the eastern Salahad made them crafty. The next reform would leave them changed to an even greater degree. The mixing of different races into the army would have made them unrecognisable to Jaher's army. However the experience and drill of their veterans forged these different groups into one force, now also driven by a common purpose: To defend and to spread the Light of the Jadd.

description.text: The Golden Highway of Jaher was the greatest infrastructure project the world had seen until that point. So great that the following generations could not keep up with its maintenance. Until the Jadd Empire stepped in and reconnected the ancient Bulwari lands with its core lands around the Mountain of Clear Sight. A new highway was constructed in the place of the old one, recreating the connection between Haless and Bulwar. Its control gave the Jadd greater power over its trade and also allowed swift movement of troops from one end of the empire to another.

description.text: The order of Lightbringers was a class of warriors, scribes, rhetoricians and clerics that had as a task to safeguard the light within the state. Their tasks mainly revolved around seeking out heathens and heretics and either making them see the light, or bringing them to trial. In the days of the Jadd Empire their powers were extended to bypass the courts and to instantly deal with anyone who did not comply with the tenets of the faith. This would lead to occasional riots and more than one instance of the burning of innocents, but it did quicken the spread of the faith within the Empire.

description.text: Since time immemorial the central question of the Bulwari religion has been how the world responds to the death or return of Surael. The Sun Cult proclaimed Jaher to be the god's reincarnation, and when he died the Sun Elves were appointed as the successors. Jaddar claimed that all people who follow the truth would be Surael's successors. In turn those who follow the Jadd see their leader as the Divine Herald and the voice of the Sun God.

player_overview.avoid_if: Avoid it if you prefer peaceful development or short campaigns, or dislike aggressive expansion, governing-capacity pressure and large-scale conversion.
player_overview.how_it_plays: Maintain the war tempo with cavalry early, form the Jadd Empire around the 150-province threshold in the middle game, then balance conquest, conversion, multi-ethnic administration and civil-war risk.
player_overview.overview: You begin as a devout Desert Elf legion and sweep across Bulwar through cavalry, zeal and continuous holy war before building a universalist religious empire that absorbs many peoples. This exceptionally long expedition keeps escalating: its expansion is exhilarating, but it also demands conversion, governing capacity, a mobile court and preparation for a civil war that may tear the empire apart.
player_overview.recommended_for: Players who enjoy exceptionally long mission trees, religious conquest, cavalry snowballing and major imperial crises.
signature_features: Legion zeal rises and falls with war, victories and conversion, and can be spent on leaders, military bonuses and cavalry reinforcement.
The mission tree crosses several continents and transforms a mobile legion into a large religious empire.
The mobile court and east–west orientation can trigger Deioderan civil war, making late administration more than continued map painting.
player_overview.tagline: Ride out to spread the one true faith, then make the transcontinental Jadd Empire real.

reasons: 21 sections and 120 directly defined missions form an exceptionally long campaign from a legion's starting position to a transcontinental empire.
After F46 forms F51, the former-F46 identity remains active; 13 of the 80 dedicated imperial missions appear only during Deioderan.
High tradition, professionalism, desert-legion zeal and cavalry interaction make expansion the central loop.
Jadd institutions, a mobile court, east–west orientation and an avoidable Deioderan crisis form a distinctive closed loop.
The endgame can avoid Deioderan; if the crisis occurs, the player can reunify diplomatically, reunify by war or accept partition.
warnings: Continuous early and mid-game war simultaneously strains manpower, administrative points, diplomatic points, money and peace windows.
Governing capacity, aggressive expansion and Deioderan's heavy penalties substantially increase the workload.
It is a poor fit for players who prefer peaceful development, overseas colonisation or a magic-and-artifice-focused everyday loop; the final route still needs a powerful mage.

values.rationale: A cross-racial universalist community, ethnic inclusion and institution-building provide clear positive value evidence; continuous holy war and forced conversion mainly reduce restraint and pluralism. Conquest and imperialisation are not independently treated as moral faults.
